W7214901089.abstract: One- and two-story wood-frame housing is the most common dwelling type in the United States. While it generally performs well in terms of earthquake life safety, certain seismic vulnerabilities, including crawlspace (cripple wall) foundations, living spaces over garages, and masonry chimneys, have led to high financial loss and displacement in past earthquakes. Building-level analyses have demonstrated significant performance differences due to foundation, garage, and chimney-related vulnerabilities, yet most regional seismic risk assessments use a single fragility function, selected based on era, to represent all wood-frame housing. Capturing the impact of specific vulnerabilities and targeted retrofit measures at the regional scale requires sufficiently detailed building inventory data. However, existing data rarely describes such features. This study addresses that gap by leveraging street-level imagery alongside Large Vision and Language Models (VLMs) to systematically collect relevant building features. Results show that VLMs can reliably screen images and identify broadly visible building features. Furthermore, this study contributes a reusable methodology for developing and evaluating prompts through repeatable strategies such as sequential questions to guide model behavior, explicit uncertainty accommodation, and assessment of uncertain or incorrect predictions, among others. While foundation types are inherently difficult to classify due to occlusions in the imagery and limitations of exterior building views, using probability-based outputs and leveraging neighborhood similarities enable nuanced assessments that could improve our understanding of exposure and uncertainty at the regional level.

W7214920731.abstract: Abstract Large language model agents can adjust optimization parameters in a treatment planning system under natural-language instruction, but no study has tested a model post-trained for extended reasoning against a general-purpose model in stereotactic radiosurgery. We compared a reasoning-optimized model (QwQ-32B) with a general-purpose model (Llama 3.1-70B) within SAGE, a locally hosted agent that adjusts optimization-objective priorities in Eclipse, which performs all optimization and dose calculation. Each configuration optimized 41 retrospective single-target brain metastasis cases (18 Gy, single fraction) with fixed clinical beam geometry; plans failing the clinical conformity standard (all but two) then received one standardized physicist instruction. The reasoning-optimized configuration produced a lower conformity ratio (median difference −0.20, 95% CI −0.48 to −0.10; $$q<0.001$$ ; lower in 36 of 41 cases) and lower normal-brain V12Gy ( $$q<0.001$$ ), improved conformity more after the instruction (difference in change −0.28, $$p<0.001$$ ), exceeded 21.6 Gy maximum dose less often (5 versus 12 plans), and produced fewer unparseable outputs (25 versus 122). Against clinical plans it showed no significant difference in PTV coverage, maximum dose, conformity ratio, or gradient index, and its right-cochlear maximum dose was lower, a clinically negligible difference.

W7214962527.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved significant advancements in natural language processing tasks, but they remain prone to generating hallucinations—outputs that are logically inconsistent or factually incorrect. While previous research has primarily focused on hallucinations in affirmative contexts, how negated contexts and knowledge lead LLMs into hallucination has received little attention. In this paper, we demonstrate that LLMs struggle to handle negation effectively, applying affirmative knowledge inappropriately, leading to hallucinations that contradict the negated input. Through a comprehensive analysis using probing protocols, we show that negated text induces previously underexplored types of hallucinations, compromising the logical consistency and factual accuracy of LLM outputs. We employ lens observations to trace, layer by layer, how Transformer-based models encode a negated input, revealing that the layer-wise prediction probabilities for pre- and post-negation inputs remain nearly indistinguishable. Additionally, our analysis extends to Korean, a morphologically distinct language, demonstrating that negation-induced hallucinations are not issues specific to English. Our findings suggest that current LLMs, across the evaluated tasks in both English and Korean, exhibit significant areas for improvement when processing negated text, raising concerns about their reliability in real-world applications. We discuss possible ways to mitigate these hallucinations, emphasizing the need for enhanced model architectures to better understand and process negation.

W7214966472.abstract: As gravitational-wave catalogs grow, they will become increasingly computationally expensive to analyze in their entirety, especially when inferring astrophysical source populations with high-dimensional, flexible models. Bayesian statistics offers a natural remedy, letting us update our knowledge of physical models as new data arrive, without re-analyzing existing data. However, doing so requires the posterior probability density of model parameters for previous observations, which is typically intractable. Here, we use variational neural posterior estimation to rapidly update the inferred population of binary black holes as data are observed in gravitational-wave detectors. We apply this approach to real and simulated catalogs analyzed with both low- and high-dimensional population models, testing the reliability of three update cadences: with new catalogs of sources, month by month during an observing run, and as each new signal arrives. We investigate the success and failure modes of neural sequential updates, finding that the robustness of updating is sensitive to the information contained in each update and that updating is most effective when performed with larger segments of data. We outline one additional scientific application enabled by Bayesian updating: identification of events that are individually informative about the population. Neural Bayesian updates to astrophysical population models also provide efficient likelihood representations for joint analyses with other data, e.g., standard-siren cosmology, and similar methods can be used to perform Bayesian stochastic background searches.

W7214986391.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) materials, including graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides, hexagonal boron nitride, and black phosphorus, have fundamentally transformed condensed matter physics and nanotechnology owing to their exceptional electronic, optical, mechanical, and thermal properties. Since the first isolation of graphene in 2004, mechanical exfoliation has remained the most reliable top-down method for producing high-quality 2D crystals. Unlike chemical vapour deposition or liquid-phase synthesis, mechanical cleavage yields pristine, single-crystal flakes with minimal defects and contamination. Over the past two decades, exfoliation techniques have evolved considerably, encompassing Scotch-tape micromechanical cleavage, polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamp-based dry transfer, and metal-assisted exfoliation using gold or other adhesion layers. These approaches have progressively improved flake size, transfer precision, and reproducibility while preserving the intrinsic crystalline quality of the parent bulk crystals. Metal-assisted exfoliation, in particular, has enabled the production of millimetre-scale monolayers on arbitrary substrates, bridging the gap between laboratory-scale research and device-oriented applications. Although scalability remains a fundamental limitation compared with bottom-up synthesis methods, recent advances in robotic automation and Bayesian optimization are addressing the inherent variability of manual exfoliation. Machine learning algorithms for automated flake identification further enhance throughput and consistency. This review summarizes the underlying principles, historical development, methodological evolution, comparative advantages, and technological challenges of mechanical exfoliation for 2D material synthesis. It also discusses future prospects, including interfacial engineering, extension to magnetic and superconducting 2D materials, and integration with heterostructure assembly, highlighting the enduring role of mechanical exfoliation in fundamental research and advanced device prototyping.

W7215063808.abstract: This paper examines the role of artificial intelligence and autonomous decision-making in the development of future pilotless combat aircraft. It uses a qualitative literature-based approach to compare human physiological and cognitive limitations with recent research on autonomous air-combat systems. Particular attention is given to high-G exposure, G-induced loss of consciousness, fatigue, cognitive workload, sensor fusion, reinforcement learning, autonomous manoeuvre decision-making, and multi-agent coordination. Existing experimental research, including the DARPA AlphaDogfight Trials and reinforcement-learning-based air-combat simulations, demonstrates that autonomous agents can perform complex tactical tasks under controlled conditions. However, these results are largely dependent on simulation and do not by themselves establish readiness for real-world operational deployment. Major challenges remain in generalisation, sim-to-real transfer, sensor reliability, verification, validation, safety assurance, and integration of multiple autonomous components. The paper also considers legal and ethical issues concerning human control, accountability, and the use of lethal autonomous systems. The findings suggest that artificial intelligence may reduce dependence on some human physiological limitations and increasingly support combat-aircraft decision-making, but near-term progress is more likely to involve human-machine teaming and gradually increasing levels of autonomy rather than an immediate transition to completely independent pilotless fighter aircraft.

W7215113648.abstract: Large artificial intelligence (AI) models are advancing rapidly across scientific and technological fields. AI-enabled big-data methods are also expanding their scope through large-scale data processing and analysis. In laboratory medicine, intelligent diagnostics based on AI integration of multi-omics and multimodal data are becoming an important direction of research. By combining different data types, investigators aim to achieve more precise disease diagnosis. Meanwhile, a new generation of diagnostic agents has emerged, such as sequential diagnostic orchestrators. In simulated cases, benchmark datasets, and controlled multispecialty evaluations, some systems have achieved diagnostic accuracy approaching or exceeding that of non-specialist physicians. These findings indicate proof-of-concept potential for coordinated decision support, but they do not establish autonomous end-to-end clinical readiness. Moreover, the central role of AI in laboratory medicine is not merely to interpret an abnormal value. It is to support the entire testing process across the pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical phases. Key applications therefore include multimodal data interpretation, discovery of new diagnostic indicators, laboratory report generation, optimization of personalized reference intervals, and development of diagnostic AI agents. Major challenges remain, including data standardization, privacy and security, model interpretability, clinical validation, and post-deployment monitoring. Research that aligns laboratory medicine with advances in AI will be an important priority over the next decade.

W7215309985.abstract: Chronic disease is one of the major causes of death worldwide which generally not vaccine preventable are also don’t resolve spontaneously. The world health organization identifies four main types of chronic diseases including cardiovascular diseases (CVD, primarily heart disease and stroke), Cancer, chronic respiratory diseases and diabetes which are responsible for the majority of related deaths, while they can be treated, are seldom healed with medicine or other medical treatment. Chronic disease care is becoming increasingly confined, which frequently results in suboptimal therapeutic efficacy and adverse medication reactions. Pharmacotherapy involve in management and treatment of chronic diseases mainly associate with the dose and drug selection for the authorized treatment that significantly impact on outcomes. Artificial intelligence and machine learning are shifting pharmacotherapy from a reactive, standardize model to proactive personalized and data driven. Different AI driven software’s and technical platform along with their superiority in management of chronic diseases has elaborate in this review article. This article looks at the use of Artificial intelligence to optimize medicine selection and dosing for complicated, long-term illness. Apart from their promising outcomes, concern about mainly data privacy, model interpretability and also ethical regulatory barriers remain. This study explores the challenges emphasizing the significant importance of transparent, explainable AI in ensuring efficacy and safety in clinical practices. The use of AI in precision pharmacology has the potential to greatly improve therapeutic results, patient compliance and healthcare resource use for chronic conditions.

W7215963294.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in private environments and accumulate valuable experience from task execution, tool use, feedback, and local knowledge. Yet such experience is distributed across organizations and cannot be directly shared because of privacy and proprietary constraints. Conventional federated learning is insufficient for this setting, as agent capabilities extend beyond model parameters to memory, tools, rewards, skills, and structured knowledge. In this paper, we formulate \textbf{Federated Agent Optimization (FAO)}, which studies how distributed agents can collaboratively improve through controlled information exchange while keeping raw data, complete trajectories, and private knowledge local. We define FAO as a multi-objective problem balancing agent utility, privacy leakage, and communication cost, and organize its optimization space across policy, memory, tool use, reward, and structured knowledge and skills. We further characterize how private experience can be abstracted, protected, aggregated, and adapted into transferable capabilities, providing a unified view of how agents can benefit from one another without direct experience sharing. Finally, we identify the key challenges of FAO and outline several promising directions for future research toward trustworthy federated agent systems.

W7216845876.abstract: The global financial landscape is undergoing a radical transformation characterized by the convergence of high-capacity computational intelligence and decentralized ledger technologies. This research explores the profound impact of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) on the evolution of financial services, moving from traditional automated systems to autonomous, self-driven entities capable of complex decision-making. By synthesizing foundational machine learning techniques in credit scoring with contemporary advancements in generative AI, the study identifies a shift from "FinTech" to "TechFin," where data-driven logic precedes financial function. The research delves into the architecture of specialized financial agents, such as FinRobot and StockAgent, examining their capacity for real-time market sentiment analysis and asset allocation. Furthermore, the article investigates the role of confidentiality-preserving blockchain systems in facilitating secure transactions within these agentic frameworks. Through an exhaustive theoretical elaboration, this work addresses the regulatory challenges and ethical considerations of delegated financial autonomy, proposing a synergistic model that integrates machine learning and agent-based modeling to enhance investment accuracy and operational efficiency. The findings suggest that while AI agents significantly augment knowledge work and underlying asset reviews, the future of financial stability depends on robust grounding mechanisms and multidisciplinary regulatory oversight.

W7217157480.abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming Knowledge Management Systems (KMS) from passive repositories of information into intelligent, adaptive, and autonomous ecosystems. This article explores the emergence of Agentic AI—AI systems capable of autonomous goal-setting, reasoning, planning, and action—and its implications for the future of knowledge management. Unlike traditional AI tools that operate reactively, Agentic AI can proactively curate, synthesize, validate, and distribute knowledge across organizational contexts. The paper examines how agent-based architectures enhance decision-making, enable dynamic knowledge orchestration, and foster continuous organizational learning. It further analyzes the integration of large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, multi-agent collaboration, and human-in-the-loop governance within next-generation KMS. Opportunities such as personalized knowledge delivery, automated expertise mapping, and cross-domain knowledge synthesis are discussed alongside challenges related to trust, transparency, ethical governance, data quality, and organizational readiness. The article concludes by proposing a conceptual framework for Agentic Knowledge Management Systems (AKMS) that balances autonomy with accountability, positioning Agentic AI as a strategic enabler of adaptive, resilient, and knowledge-driven enterprises. W7217384963.abstract: The rapid maturation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transitioned from narrow, task-specific applications to autonomous "agentic" systems capable of complex reasoning, adaptive resource management, and high-stakes decision-making. This research article explores the multi-faceted evolution of AI through the lens of Agentic AI, Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), and Large Language Models (LLMs) integrated with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). By synthesizing contemporary literature across healthcare, finance, and industrial automation, this study delineates the architectural requirements for hierarchical multi-modal systems and the socio-technical implications of machines as teammates. We specifically examine the "Agentic Turn," wherein AI systems move beyond passive response to proactive, self-driven goal pursuit. The analysis covers the technical efficiency of performance-optimized LLM fusion, the necessity of explainability and "causability" in medical diagnostics, and the economic shifts precipitated by autonomous self-driving technology. Furthermore, the paper addresses the critical intersection of federated learning and data privacy in decentralized agent networks. Theoretical frameworks for human-artificial interaction are scrutinized to identify the transition from tool-use to systemic collaboration. The findings suggest that while Agentic AI offers unprecedented gains in industrial efficiency and personalized service, its successful implementation depends on robust hierarchical architectures, rigorous explainability standards, and an ethical rethinking of process mining. This comprehensive review provides a roadmap for future research in autonomous cyber-physical systems, emphasizing the shift toward adaptive, trust-based AI ecosystems.

W7219686172.abstract: Machine learning has made significant contributions to the fields of chemistry and materials science, enabling the exploration of vast chemical space through large-scale quantum chemical calculations. These models provide fast and accurate predictions of atomistic chemical properties, but they have limitations when it comes to capturing the electronic degrees of freedom of a molecule. This restricts their application in reactive chemistry and chemical analysis. To address this limitation, we introduce a deep learning framework that predicts the quantum mechanical wavefunction of a molecule in a local basis of atomic orbitals. The wavefunction serves as a foundational representation from which all other ground-state properties can be derived. Our approach maintains complete access to the electronic structure through the wavefunction, while achieving computational efficiency comparable to force-field methods. Moreover, the framework captures quantum mechanics in a form that can be analytically differentiated, allowing for efficient optimization and exploration of chemical systems. We demonstrate the potential of our approach through several examples. By leveraging the predicted wavefunction, we showcase the ability to perform inverse design of molecular structures to target specific electronic property optimizations. This opens exciting avenues for tailoring molecular structures to achieve desired electronic characteristics. Additionally, our framework paves the way for enhanced synergy between machine learning and quantum chemistry, enabling more comprehensive investigations into complex chemical systems.

W7219939203.abstract: This paper presented an empirical investigation into the hyperparameter optimization of the Meta LLaMA 3.2 3B Instruct model, conducted during the POLYCC LLM League 2025 competition. The study utilized a parameter-efficient fine-tuning approach via AWS SageMaker Jumpstart to adapt the artificial intelligence for specialized conversational tasks. The research demonstrated a critical disconnect between traditional computer science metrics specifically training and evaluation loss and the actual conversational success rate, measured as Win Rate (WR). Experimental data revealed that minimizing training loss to near-zero on small datasets (under 500 examples) induced catastrophic overfitting, severely degrading the chatbot's real-world performance to as low as 10%. The optimal configuration was identified at a moderate dataset scale of 1000 examples trained for 20 epochs, achieving a peak Win Rate of 36%.

W7219972064.abstract: Organoids and organ-on-a-chip technologies have emerged as transformative platforms in modern biomedical research, offering new approaches for studying human biology, disease mechanisms, drug development, toxicity assessment, and personalized medicine. Conventional experimental systems, including two-dimensional cell cultures and animal models, have generated substantial scientific knowledge but often fail to reproduce the structural, cellular, mechanical, and biochemical complexity of human tissues and organs. Organoids are three-dimensional, self-organizing cellular structures that reproduce selected architectural and functional characteristics of organs. Organ-on-a-chip systems, in contrast, use microengineering and microfluidics to recreate aspects of human tissue physiology within controlled miniature platforms. Both technologies seek to bridge the gap between simplified laboratory models and human biological systems. This research paper examines the scientific foundations of organoids and organ-on-a-chip technologies and evaluates their applications in cancer research, infectious diseases, drug discovery, pharmacology, toxicology, regenerative medicine, and precision medicine. Particular attention is given to patient-derived organoids, multi-organ chips, microfluidic systems, vascularization, mechanical stimulation, and the integration of artificial intelligence. The paper also explores the complementary relationship between organoids and organ-on-a-chip platforms. While organoids provide complex three-dimensional cellular organization, organ-on-a-chip technologies offer precise control of fluid flow, mechanical forces, oxygen gradients, and tissue interfaces. Their integration may create increasingly sophisticated human-relevant models. Nevertheless, limitations remain, including incomplete maturation, lack of full physiological complexity, reproducibility problems, vascular and immune-system limitations, technical standardization, manufacturing costs, and regulatory uncertainty. Future developments are expected to integrate stem-cell biology, tissue engineering, microfluidics, artificial intelligence, single-cell sequencing, spatial biology, and personalized medicine. The convergence of these technologies could substantially improve the prediction of human responses to diseases and therapeutics while reducing dependence on traditional experimental models.

W7220241472.abstract: The deployment of large language models as autonomous agents has demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language understanding, reasoning, and tool use. However, when multiple such agents operate in partially observable environments, their ability to coordinate effectively is often bottlenecked by the inefficiencies of standard natural language communication and the cognitive load of processing high-dimensional contextual information. This paper investigates the phenomenon of emergent symbolic communication among large language model agents tasked with cooperative problem-solving under strict partial observability. We propose a novel cognitive architecture that incentivizes agents to compress complex environmental states and reasoning trajectories into discrete, compositional symbolic representations. Through extensive empirical analysis across decentralized decision-making tasks, we demonstrate that agents can autonomously develop a highly efficient, context-dependent symbolic vocabulary that significantly outperforms standard natural language protocols in both transmission efficiency and coordination success rates. Furthermore, we provide a rigorous theoretical framework grounded in information theory to model the symbolic compression process. Our findings reveal that the emergent language exhibits structural properties akin to natural languages, such as Zipfian distribution and compositionality, while being heavily optimized for the specific constraints of the environment. This research advances the understanding of multi-agent coordination, offering a scalable methodology for deploying robust, bandwidth-efficient agent swarms in complex, real-world scenarios.

Through a multilayer process, it gains complex image understanding using deep learning methods for video understanding, implemented by converting images to text. In this study, the system extracts video frames, then processes them using the Transformer and Inception V3 architectures for image captioning. This synchronization is based on the Multitask Deep Learning method, which combines a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for the image area, a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) with LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) for the sentence area, a Caption Content Network (CCN), and a Relational Network (RCN). Context). We use the Transformer Encoder-Decoder architecture to label objects and model relationships between them. To test image-to-text conversion, we use scores to compare the predicted text with one or more reference translations, along with accuracy and loss validation tables and graphs showing epoch-by-epoch loss. For the image dataset from the CNN features, it will immediately enter multitask learning along with text classification; the score will be calculated, and the result will be image caption text. Future research should examine the generalization gap by assessing both validation loss and training loss. W7220693122.abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a clinical syndrome defined by shared manifestations but produced by diverse combinations of cardiometabolic, vascular, inflammatory, renal, pulmonary, atrial, skeletal-muscle, and aging-related mechanisms. This heterogeneity limits the value of classifications based only on left ventricular ejection fraction and helps explain why many mechanistically plausible interventions have produced neutral average results. Deep phenotyping can move the field from descriptive heterogeneity toward biologically coherent and clinically actionable subtypes by integrating clinical trajectories, advanced imaging, exercise and invasive hemodynamics, circulating biomarkers, multiomics, and digital physiology. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers methods to combine these high-dimensional data, but statistical clusters should not be equated with disease endotypes. A useful subtype must be reproducible across cohorts, anchored to plausible biology, associated with a distinct clinical course, and able to improve diagnosis, therapeutic selection, or clinical-trial design. This Review examines the translational continuum from experimental HFpEF models to human patient subtypes, summarizes the main deep-phenotyping domains and AI approaches, and proposes seven clinically interpretable subtype families: cardiometabolic-inflammatory, hypertensive-vascular aging, atrial myopathy, pulmonary vascular-right ventricular, cardiorenal-congestive, peripheral-frailty, and specific etiologic phenocopies. Current evidence supports a layered treatment strategy in which broadly effective therapies, particularly sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, are combined with phenotype-directed management of obesity, diabetes, mineralocorticoid receptor activation, atrial fibrillation, congestion, pulmonary vascular disease, and physical deconditioning. The central next step is prospective validation of dynamic subtype assignments in external populations and phenotype-enriched trials. Phenogroup labels should therefore be regarded as pragmatic, transitional proxies for dominant mechanisms when those mechanisms cannot yet be measured directly at the individual-patient level; their value lies in improving decisions while the field moves toward fully individualized mechanism-based treatment. Deep phenotyping will be clinically valuable only when it changes a decision and improves an outcome, rather than merely increasing descriptive complexity.

W7220697510.abstract: Background: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) involves vascular remodeling and altered mechanical signaling. The immune-associated transcriptomic changes accompanying this environment remain incompletely characterized. Methods: We integrated bulk lung (GSE15197), PBMC (GSE33463), and single-cell RNA-seq (GSE169471) data using a curated set of 2, 537 mechanical-related genes. WGCNA, LASSO, random forest, and single-cell localization supported candidate prioritization. The four-gene panel was examined in a monocrotaline-induced PH rat model and PBMCs from 10 IPAH patients and 10 controls. Results: PAH transcriptomes showed enrichment of stress-fiber, actomyosin, ECM, and immune-related programs. CD83, CD86, IL6, and TLR7 were prioritized, with compartment-dependent expression patterns. Single-cell data localized CD83/CD86 to myeloid/APC compartments and IL6 to endothelial/fibroblast populations; TLR7 was sparsely detected. In MCT-treated rat lungs, CD86 and TLR7 proteins increased, whereas CD83 and IL-6 decreased. Clinical PBMCs showed corresponding expression directions, and each gene had an AUC >0.7. The exploratory four-gene disease-state score achieved an internal cross-validated AUC of 0.765. Conclusions: The four candidates provide a cellular and molecular context for investigating immune-stromal interactions in PAH, including responses to noninfectious vascular injury. The panel showed moderate internal discrimination. These findings support further clinical and functional investigation but do not establish direct mechanotransduction targets or a causal pathway linking mechanical stress to vascular inflammation.

W7220733556.abstract: Recently Large Language Models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents increasingly need to incorporate knowledge acquired after pretraining, e.g., domain facts, user preferences, documents, and interaction experience. In-context learning (ICL) and ICL-based agent harness remain flexible, but they consume context capacity and incur repeated discretized encoding cost that grows with context length. \textbf{In-parameter memory} offers a complementary substrate: reusable memory information is represented in model parameters, adapters, or other parameter-like objects that are composed into the forward pass at inference time. This survey focuses on methods that augment LLMs with such parametric memory at deployment: a memory-bearing parameter object is plugged into the forward pass during inference, whether it is acquired before or during deployment. We organize the landscape with two orthogonal axes: \textbf{Parameter Placement}, which includes Embedding, Attention, FFN layers, or Hybrid when two or more layers are used; and \textbf{Parameter Acquisition Time}, which distinguishes methods whose memory object is acquired during deployment (online) from those acquired before it (offline). We clarify boundaries, conduct comparisons, and discuss open directions in interference, safety, co-design with ICL, and recursive self-improvement.

W7220773754.abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models has fundamentally transformed natural language processing, yet their application in highly specialized domains remains constrained by inherent limitations such as hallucination, lack of verifiable sourcing, and temporal knowledge degradation. Retrieval-augmented generation has emerged as a promising paradigm to address these vulnerabilities by grounding model responses in external, continuously updated knowledge bases. However, evaluating the efficacy and robustness of these systems in specialized fields such as medicine, law, and finance requires comprehensive benchmarks and a nuanced understanding of failure modes. This paper introduces a novel, domain-specific question answering benchmark designed explicitly to stress-test retrieval-augmented architectures. Furthermore, we propose a comprehensive error taxonomy that systematically categorizes failures into distinct retrieval, generation, and reasoning inadequacies. Through extensive empirical analysis of multiple state-of-the-art models, we reveal that while retrieval augmentation significantly reduces factual hallucination, it introduces new classes of errors, particularly related to context fragmentation and semantic misalignment. The proposed taxonomy provides a foundational framework for diagnosing system bottlenecks, thereby guiding future research toward more reliable, transparent, and accurate domain-specific question answering systems.

W7220782072.abstract: The discipline of software quality assurance is undergoing a profound evolutionary transition as the rapid contraction of vulnerability weaponization timelines renders traditional manual testing and rigid programmatic scripting obsolete. This review article provides an exhaustive analysis of the paradigm shift brought by Large Language Models (LLMs) from automating repetitive testing actions to automating complex cognitive processes. We categorize foundational code-aware model architectures into encoder-only, encoder-decoder, and decoder-only archetypes, evaluating their trade-offs across execution latency, logical reasoning, and context window capacities. Furthermore, we analyze state-of-the-art automated test generation frameworks that integrate structural program analysis, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and execution feedback loops, while highlighting the ongoing debate regarding whether LLMs possess true semantic reasoning capabilities or merely replicate memorized surface-level code patterns. In the realm of software security, this paper evaluates neuro-symbolic detection frameworks that combine the high recall of LLMs with the precision of static application security testing tools. We explore precision vulnerability localization techniques, including attention rectification mechanisms and agentic trace analysis, which resolve traditional granularity dilemmas by pinpointing line-level defects. Finally, we examine the evolution of automated program repair from brittle generate-and-validate templates into conversational, multi-turn feedback loops and autonomous multi-agent cyber-reasoning systems that utilize the Model Context Protocol and ReAct-style execution histories. Ultimately, this review establishes that while AI-driven testing introduces non-deterministic behaviors and security risks, its integration into autonomous lifecycles yields unprecedented efficiency, as demonstrated by the automated discovery and patching of real-world zero-day vulnerabilities in active critical infrastructure.

W7220784439.abstract: The numerical resolution of high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) represents a long-standing challenge in computational mathematics and engineering due to the exponential complexity scale of traditional mesh-based methods. This review paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the co-evolution and mathematical foundations of deep learning-based, mesh-free PDE solvers designed to break this curse of dimensionality. We systematically examine three prominent computational paradigms: PDE-residual-based approaches, stochastic methods, and variational/weak formulation frameworks. Specifically, we investigate how Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) integrate physical laws directly into multi-task loss functions, while highlighting advanced adaptive weighting and geometry-aware schemes designed to mitigate optimization stiffness and gradient pathologies. Furthermore, the survey evaluates stochastic formulations notably the Deep Backward Stochastic Differential Equation (BSDE) framework which reformulate parabolic equations into stochastic learning tasks evaluated along simulated Brownian paths, establishing rigorous error bounds even for non-Lipschitz generators. We also explore variational methods like the Deep Ritz Method (DRM) and Weak Adversarial Networks (WAN) that minimize physical energy functionals or leverage minimax optimization to handle non-self-adjoint operators. Finally, this paper reviews cutting-edge scaling methodologies designed for ultra-high-dimensional domains exceeding 100,000 dimensions, such as Separable PINNs (SPINN) utilizing forward-mode automatic differentiation and Stochastic Dimension Gradient Descent (SDGD). Quantitative benchmarks across fifteen systems demonstrate that these deep learning architectures remain physically consistent while delivering up to a 72% computational cost reduction compared to classical finite element methods. Ultimately, this review maps the bidirectional synergy between mathematical theory and domain-specific engineering applications, outlining future pathways for scientific machine learning.

W7220960503.abstract: Large language models are increasingly embedded in agentic software systems that retrieve information, plan subtasks, call tools, modify code, execute tests, and adapt through memory or feedback. This transition changes the safety problem: when a model acts through software tools, failure can alter external state. This Perspective argues that agentic AI safety should move beyond exclusive reliance on model trust, alignment, or prompt-level defenses and should also be treated as a software-architecture problem. We propose software topology as a design lens for structurally governed autonomy and develop a five-plane reference topology comprising intent, orchestration, execution, oversight, and adaptation. Its core invariant is that components that decide should not directly act, and components that act should not act without supervision. The topology is realized in Polos, an open reference specification that encodes role contracts, message schemas, declared flow graphs, bounded loops, governed self-improvement, and validator-checked invariants. We argue that this approach complements model alignment and empirical red teaming by providing an inspectable substrate for evaluating, constraining, and governing tool-using AI agents.

W7221020762.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as reasoning engines within multi-step, tool-using agent pipelines, yet their value for core recommendation tasks relative to classical collaborative filtering (CF) remains poorly characterized. We present an agentic recommender system for the MovieLens-100K dataset that decomposes recommendation into four cooperating agents: a Planner that converts free-text user requests into structured intent, a Retriever that performs deterministic, tool-based candidate generation via singular value decomposition (SVD), a Ranker/Explainer that selects and justifies a final list using a locally hosted Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model, and a Critic that verifies genre-exclusion constraints and can trigger a bounded retry loop. We evaluate the system along four axes: ranking accuracy (Hit@K, NDCG@K) against Random, Popularity, and CF-only baselines; constraint-satisfaction rate under free-text exclusion requests; automatic groundedness of generated explanations; and end-to-end latency. On a leave-one-out protocol with n = 600 evaluation users, the agentic pipeline achieves Hit@10 = 0.120 and NDCG@10 = 0.059, closely approaching the pure SVD baseline (Hit@10 = 0.130, NDCG@10 = 0.060) while substantially outperforming Popularity (Hit@10 = 0.030) and Random (Hit@10 = 0.002) baselines. Uniquely, the agentic pipeline achieves a 0.28% constraint-violation rate across 712 recommendations spanning 500 constrained queries, and 95.05% of generated explanations are automatically verified as grounded in the recommended movie's true genre metadata – capabilities that CF-only, Popularity, and Random baselines cannot provide by construction. We report this latency overhead honestly (≈ 23.7s per user versus ≈ 0.001s for CF-only, a ∼19,300× difference) and discuss the implications for deployment. Our findings suggest that LLM-based re-ranking of an already-strong retriever does not straightforwardly improve ranking accuracy, but adds genuinely new, verifiable capabilities – constraint adherence and natural-language explanation – that are structurally unavailable to classical recommenders.

W7221518687.abstract: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.

W7221541683.abstract: Language models increasingly support or automate information retrieval from document collections too large to index. This task is difficult when it requires specialist linguistic or scientific knowledge. We used the Wikipedia Game to test language models on an analogous information retrieval task. In the game, players must reach a target article using only article links. We compared sentence embedding models and LLMs across five Wikipedia languages and five academic-literature datasets. We construct very large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and of paper citations using OpenAlex and provide code to build and navigate them. This allows the study of language models' navigation capabilities without relying on third-party APIs. We compared the models with human and TF-IDF benchmarks. The Wikipedia Game format enables robust comparisons across techniques, languages, and domains. No model significantly outperformed humans, although the best models (GPT-o3 mini, GPT-4o, QwQ:32B, and DeepSeek-R1:70B) achieved comparable success. Performance and rankings varied across languages and topics, with implications for practitioners utilising these techniques.

W7221543823.abstract: Designing tool-integrated reasoning agent systems for complex chemical tasks remains a fundamental challenge. Although recent chemical agents have demonstrated promising performance through the integration of external tools, they are still built on the autoregressive paradigm, which is inherently constrained by causal attention and left-to-right generation. As a result, they often struggle with bidirectional molecular understanding, global coordinated tool planning and multi-source evidence integration. To address this challenge, we introduce ChemDiffAgent, the first masked diffusion language agent for tool-integrated chemical reasoning. It reformulates chemical reasoning as iterative denoising over interleaved reasoning and tool-use trajectories, enabling tool-use decisions to be jointly determined under full-trajectory context and thereby better aligning the agent's decision boundary with its knowledge boundary. We further analyze how this paradigm benefits agentic reasoning through harder infilling subproblems during training and flexible arbitrary-order decoding during inference. Then we develop a two-stage post-training framework, comprising agentic supervised fine-tuning and variance-reduced preference optimization, to enhance tool-use and reasoning capabilities. We also construct a comprehensive benchmark covering six chemistry tasks across both single-turn and multi-turn tool-use scenarios. Under matched budgets and evaluation, ChemDiffAgent consistently outperforms autoregressive agents, achieving an overall improvement of approximately 20%. Notably, our 8B model achieves performance comparable to, in some cases surpassing, significantly larger frontier models, such as GPT 5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. Code is available at https://github.com/bilemond/ChemDiffAgent.

W7221590255.abstract: Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) have revolutionized the management of high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC). Yet, current treatment decisions remain almost exclusively guided by static BRCA/homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) genotyping. This paradigm is increasingly challenged by a profound eligibility-benefit gap: real-world data show 93.4% of patients are PARPi-eligible, but only 22.0% achieve meaningful 2-year progression-free survival benefit, compounded by 10-30% HRD test failure rates, inability to capture dynamic resistance evolution, and negligible predictive value in the ~50% of HGSOC that are homologous recombination-proficient. This narrative review, based on literature up to June 2026, systematically evaluates functional biomarkers that complement BRCA/HRD testing by assessing real-time tumor biology. To our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate these biomarkers into a unified whole-disease-course framework accounting for evidence level, assay cost, and global resource setting. RAD51 immunohistochemistry directly visualizes homologous recombination repair capacity, achieving 95% accuracy in predicting PARPi response in preclinical patient-derived xenograft models and demonstrating robust predictive value in prospective clinical cohorts. The KELIM model, derived from early CA-125 kinetics and evaluated in >12,000 patients within prospective trial and registry datasets, provides a no-additional-assay-cost, tissue-independent readout of chemosensitivity with potential for broad, low-cost global deployment. Circulating tumor DNA enables noninvasive longitudinal monitoring of resistance, potentially preceding radiographic progression by weeks to months. Exploratory immune and artificial intelligence-based multimodal markers further refine response stratification. We propose deployment of these biomarkers at four critical clinical nodes-diagnosis, post-chemotherapy, maintenance, and progression-to guide therapy selection dynamically. By transitioning from static genotype-based eligibility to real-time functional phenotyping, this integrated strategy aims to close the eligibility-benefit gap and advance adaptive precision oncology for ovarian cancer globally. As a narrative review, this work aims to offer forward-looking conceptual frameworks and stimulate future research rather than to establish high-level clinical evidence or formal guidelines.

W7221614473.abstract: Abstract Synthetic tabular data generation plays a key role in alleviating data scarcity and privacy limitations in machine learning, especially in regulated domains such as finance and healthcare. While many existing methods focus on producing realistic and predictive tabular data, fairness is often not explicitly considered, leading to biased synthetic datasets. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) further enhance data quality through natural language representations, which underscores the need for principled mechanisms that ensure fairness alongside predictive performance. To address this challenge, we propose SENNA, a framework that integrates disentangled semantic representations with LLM-based generation to jointly preserve utility and improve fairness. The framework separates task-relevant and task-independent information in the latent space and leverages these representations to guide generation and validation. Experimental results on three real-world datasets show that SENNA achieves competitive downstream performance, while substantially reducing both group-level disparities and individual-level inequality. We further evaluate the framework across multiple backbones, providing insights into fairness–utility trade-offs in LLM-based tabular data synthesis.

W7221663374.abstract: We propose FedChainDP, a federated learning framework that combines update-level noise perturbation with blockchain audit logging for privacy-preserving collaborative ECG classification across multiple healthcare institutions. Healthcare institutions face a fundamental tension: deep learning models require large, diverse training datasets to achieve high diagnostic accuracy, yet strict privacy regulations such as HIPAA and GDPR restrict the sharing of raw patient data across organizational boundaries. FedChainDP resolves this tension by enabling hospitals to collaboratively train a shared CNN model without exchanging raw electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. Each hospital trains locally on its private data and shares only noise-perturbed model updates, to which Gaussian noise is added once per federated round; these updates are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before transmission and logged on an immutable blockchain with Merkle-tree integrity protection and smart-contract policy checks on the reported noise parameters. Because this round-level noise schedule does not satisfy the assumptions of the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant, the accountant output for the main configuration (ε_nom = 7.84 at δ = 10⁻⁵) is reported only as a nominal indicator, and no formal (ε, δ)-differential privacy guarantee is claimed. We evaluate FedChainDP on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia dataset partitioned across 5 hospitals using Dirichlet-based non-IID distributions. Our CNN model achieves 98.91% ± 0.14% accuracy under federated learning with update-level noise injection (σ_mult = 1.1), compared to 98.81% ± 0.31% for centralized training and 98.57% ± 0.17% for federated learning without noise-based privacy protection. These accuracies were obtained under a beat-level random split performed after duplication-based class balancing, so duplicated minority-class beats and beats from the same patients can occur in both training and test sets; they therefore reflect performance within this resampled benchmark and do not establish generalization to independent unseen beats or patients. A comprehensive privacy-utility analysis across noise multiplier settings (σ_multiplier ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 100}) demonstrates that classification accuracy remains above 98% across all evaluated noise levels. A black-box membership inference attack achieved 50.28% accuracy (near random guessing) against the noise-perturbed model; however, comparable near-chance accuracy was also obtained against the models trained without noise (49.16% centralized; 49.48% federated), so this result neither isolates a benefit of the noise mechanism nor substitutes for a formal privacy guarantee. A single-machine scalability simulation across 2 to 20 simulated hospitals produced accuracies of 98.90% (2 hospitals), 95.10% (5 hospitals), 93.80% (10 hospitals), and 97.20% (20 hospitals), respectively, while the simulated blockchain audit trail adds negligible overhead (0.059–0.091 s average mining time per block within the single-machine environment). FedChainDP incorporates technical safeguards relevant to healthcare privacy and accountability objectives across four dimensions: multi-technique privacy integration, blockchain-logged policy checks on reported noise parameters, smart contract access control, and empirical membership-inference evaluation.

W7221772943.abstract: As agentic artificial intelligence evolves from task-oriented automation to persistent organizational participation, existing multi-agent frameworks offer limited guidance on enterprise governance, institutional continuity, and accountability. This conceptual paper proposes the Hierarchical Agentic AI Governance Architecture (HAAGA), which organizes an Autonomous AI Organization across Governance, Administration, Operations, and Organizational Memory. An Autonomous AI Organization is distinguished from a persistent multi-agent system by an enduring mission and identity; durable departments, roles, and decision rights; formal escalation and final adjudication; institutional governance; controlled organizational memory; continuity across agent replacement; and auditable accountability. Decisions remain at the lowest level, with formally assigned authority and validated competence, while unresolved disagreements, insufficient authority, or requests for guidance trigger escalation from local to supervisory and executive levels. The Board of AI Governors and Executive AI are organizational roles that may be implemented by autonomous agents, human officials, or hybrid arrangements; the sponsoring legal organization and a designated human officer retain accountability for consequential decisions. HAAGA preserves departmental recommendations, evidence, reasoning, objections, and revisions in a controlled, versioned decision record that informs future cases. Preserved dissent improves reviewability but does not by itself create independent perspectives when departments share models, data, tools, or policy constraints. HAAGA therefore offers a theory-informed organizational specification whose effectiveness, scalability, and bias-mitigation properties require prototype implementation and empirical evaluation.

W7221793147.abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.

W7221803962.abstract: In this study, an artificial intelligence-assisted evaluation of the refractive indices of different materials is performed. The evaluation of the refractive index is necessary to design photonic devices for various classical and quantum photonic applications, and to theoretically analyse experimental results. The refractive index is one of the crucial parameters that affect the interaction of light with matter. Although the refractive index can be measured experimentally, its estimation via computational means provide the advantage of not requiring costly instrumentation, trained researchers and could avoid potential laboratory-based uncertainties. Therefore, in this study, artificial intelligence is implemented to estimate the optical constants of two types of materials, i.e., noble metals, and semiconductors. To this end, an artificial neural network is used to estimate the real and the imaginary parts of the refractive index of a specific material for various wavelengths of light. Then, the knowledge of the trained neural network is employed to initiate and train new neural networks to estimate the refractive indices of other materials. For the training of a neural network, various methods can be deployed. However, the application of the training can be a time-consuming process. A transfer learning approach is here implemented to provide a faster training solution for the problem under study. The implementation of transfer learning allows training the neural networks for a new material with higher speed or accuracy when compared to non-knowledge transfer-based training. Our results show the efficiency of the proposed technique in accurately evaluating the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index of different materials.

W7222158066.abstract: Machine learning can build near-optimal summary statistics for extracting cosmological information from the large-scale structure of the Universe. Training them, however, requires large numbers of costly simulations. We aim to build a neural summary trained on fast, approximate low-resolution simulations that remains informative when applied to higher-resolution ones, reducing the cost of the training set. We train an ensemble of convolutional neural networks with different architectures to compress the matter overdensity fields of low-resolution particle-mesh simulations. The outputs of a subset of networks are concatenated into a summary statistic, which we use to constrain $Ω_{\rm m}$ and $σ_8$ from high-resolution particle-mesh simulations, each about a thousand times more costly than their low-resolution counterparts. Theoretical predictions are provided by a Gaussian process emulator built from the high-resolution simulations. We test three strategies for selecting the smallest informative subset of networks. Constraints are compared with those from a reference power spectrum analysis. We also consider dark matter halo catalogues from independent high-resolution $N$-body simulations. The neural summary extracts information beyond the binned power spectrum. Using multiple networks is essential: a single network can be less informative than the power spectrum. A greedy search based on posterior volume provides the tightest constraints with the fewest networks. The neural summary also outperforms the power spectrum for dark matter haloes, at different number densities and redshifts, despite being trained on low-resolution matter fields at $z=0$. This work demonstrates that an ensemble of networks trained on approximate simulations yields a summary statistic that remains informative on higher-fidelity data, including dark matter haloes. W7222345891.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can self-evolve at test time by accumulating experience: retrieving relevant memories before acting and writing new lessons back afterwards. Yet most are single-level: trajectories, distilled workflows and reasoning items all land in one undifferentiated pool indexed by embedding similarity, with no typed abstraction hierarchy. They never forget or deduplicate, and are prone to negative transfer, where a superficially similar but directionally opposite experience is recalled and its concrete steps are copied verbatim, actively harming the agent. We introduce STRATA, a structured, outcome-grounded, self-maintaining memory that organizes experience into a three-layer graph of atomic skills and code snippets, task workflows and generalized meta-frameworks, connected by typed edges. STRATA maintains itself through five mechanisms sharing one similarity geometry: a multi-dimensional similarity that scores retrieval by operation and target; a typed reflector crystallizing procedures from successes and pitfalls from failures; community detection that induces meta-frameworks; pressure-triggered garbage collection with articulation-point protection; and contrast edges that flag confusable, direction-opposite experiences. Across four interactive benchmarks (AppWorld, WebArena, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld), two frozen backbones and seven baselines, STRATA attains the best average score while simultaneously using the lowest latency and fewest environment steps of any memory-augmented method, and 44% fewer lines of injected memory than the most context-hungry baseline. We isolate two failure modes of prior memories: single-level memory degrades sharply as the task set grows, and single-level concrete memories suffer catastrophic negative transfer, which contrast edges repair, lifting ScienceWorld from 78.7 to 96.7 within the same system.

W7222405865.abstract: The high stakes governance decision making that is being mediated by autonomous artificial intelligence agents in regulatory compliance, financial services and millions of citizens in public administration are increasing.The transformational advantages of high computational efficiency are offset by the lack of accountability that accompanies the transparency of autonomous agents which harms the trust and compliance with regulations.The survey conducts a synthesis of 127 peer-reviewed (2020-2025) articles that discuss the frameworks of the design of trustful and explicable agentic AI systems to governance issues.We examine 43 cases of implementation in seven areas of governance and introduce the Trustworthy and Explainable Agent Governance (TEAG) architect ure: a fivelayer data governance, agent coordination, explainability, accountability infrastructure, and human -supervision system.Empirically, agentic AI systems that have transparency and accountability built into them have an average transparency improvement of 63 percent, compliance rate of 91 percent, and sustain a 5.2x efficiency benefit over human decision-making.It is analyzed that decision transparency requires not only the explainability techniques, but also architectural integration in both governance and technical, as well as organizational aspects.This essay offers evidence-based recommendations to adopting governance quality agentic AI systems that are autonomous and democratic at the same time.

W7222791600.abstract: This paper presents a conceptual review of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI), autonomous agents, and multi-agent system security. It discusses key security threats, including prompt injection, excessive tool permissions, sensitive data leakage, memory poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, and cascading failures. The paper proposes a layered security framework incorporating identity management, least-privilege access, policy-controlled tool usage, secure agent communication, memory protection, monitoring, bounded autonomy, and human approval for high-impact actions. It also outlines an evaluation methodology using adversarial test cases and measurable security and performance metrics. This work aims to support the development of safer, more reliable, and secure agentic AI systems. The proposed framework is conceptual and literature-based; no prototype implementation or experimental results are claimed.

W7222955960.abstract: Building a correct, performant HPC simulation from a scientific idea demands scarce, largely implicit expertise in numerical methods and library APIs. AI agents can now draft such code, but a draft that looks right is not necessarily one that an engineer can trust. We take a research-software-engineering (RSE) view of a real fusion-energy problem: not whether AI can replace that expertise, but what an RSE must build around a multi-agent AI system (orchestration, verification gates, provenance, and guardrails) to make its output trustworthy. Using a multi-agent AI system, from a plain-language prompt, we generate a PETSc simulation of the tokamak Grad–Shafranov equilibrium for nuclear fusion energy. In this poster, we will present the PETSc multi-agent system and demonstrate its application on this problem. The system includes a mathematical modeling agent, a numerical analysis agent, and an HPC code generation and execution agent. Around them, there is a project-owned orchestration driver that records every artifact (model, discretization decision, generated source code, build / run logs) with full provenance, so that runs are reproducible, resumable, and auditable. There is also a verification harness that gates every result before it is accepted. From the prompt (“Grad–Shafranov equilibrium for magnetically confined plasma in a tokamak”), the mathematical modeling agent identified the governing equation and returned its strong and weak forms; the numerical analysis agent selected a nonlinear solver on a structured grid; and the HPC code generation and execution agent produced a compact PETSc program that discretizes the operator on a distributed array with a true Jacobian matrix, and embeds a method-of-manufactured-solutions check. We do not treat “it compiled and ran” as sufficient evidence of success: an MPI-parallel grid-refinement study confirms second-order convergence. Verification, not the model’s confidence, decides acceptance. The same pipeline then produced one parameterized solver for several real-machine-shaped equilibria. Each was verified against an exact analytic benchmark and cross-checked against an independent community code. We scaled from the toy anchor to trustworthy shaped cases without re-architecting the generated solver. Running the AI agents on a shared HPC machine took environment and dependency wrangling, working-directory-independent process spawning, and graceful degradation when optional components were absent. There are also guardrails: in one instructive failure, a hard-coded iteration cap in the built-in orchestrator mislabeled a genuinely successful multi-stage run as a failure. We diagnosed it and contributed the fix upstream. Human effort is not eliminated but relocated, from writing solver code to engineering the orchestration, verification, and guardrails that make an AI system’s output trustworthy and its failures legible. We report per-run decision-gate metrics: correctness (model identified, program compiled and ran, convergence order), efficiency (execution duration, LLM / tool calls), and where human effort went (as a lightweight, reusable way to evaluate an agentic workflow rather than merely admire its output). The contribution is a candid, verification-driven account of how a research software engineer can wrap multi-agent AI code generation so that it produces trustworthy HPC simulation code for a flagship fusion-energy problem, and of the guardrails needed when it does not. In future work, we will raise the simulation difficulty to nonlinear profiles, time-dependent and resistive magnetohydrodynamics, and three-dimensional tokamak plasma, to map where the system succeeds and where it breaks, and to design guardrails and human-in-the-loop checkpoints that keep engineers in control as problems get harder.

W7223024386.abstract: We study feature vectors: directions in a language model's activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can causally steer model behavior when injected into activations. We further use these features to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical and agentic reasoning. Our targeted feature construction thus offers a scalable route to studying concepts in language models, potentially extending to millions of features across arbitrary domains.

W7223078329.abstract: Integrated Remote Operation Centres (IROCs) are emerging as the architectural frontier of Industry 4.0 for capital-intensive sectors such as mining, oil and gas, and energy. Yet two intertwined gaps constrain their evolution towards full autonomy. First, no integrated agentic architecture has been proposed for mining IROCs that orchestrates Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition systems, digital twins, predictive analytics and human-machine interfaces under safety-critical constraints. Second, no evaluation framework jointly addresses the real-time, Health-Safety-Environment, regulatory-auditability and cost-per-decision requirements that govern industrial agentic deployments. This paper makes four contributions. It synthesises industry needs and quantified gains documented in analogous industries that motivate an agentic approach to mining IROCs. It introduces EI2ROC, a three-tier multi-agent architecture combining a Large Language Model orchestrator with specialised monitoring and production-capacityprediction agents communicating through a Model Context Protocol-style tool interface. It provides a critical review of agentic evaluation along six orthogonal dimensions and identifies the industrial blind spot of current benchmarks. Finally, it proposes a multi-dimensional benchmarking framework for industrial agentic AI comprising scenario library, harness, metrics and humancalibration protocol. The paper states explicitly which components are implemented in the current prototype, which belong to the proposed reference design and which remain future work, and reports preliminary cost and latency observations from an operating site. Together, EI2ROC and the benchmarking framework constitute a methodological blueprint transferable across CAPEX intensive industries.

W7223078747.abstract: Artificial intelligence is moving beyond prediction, content generation, and decision support into systems that plan, select tools, communicate with external parties, and execute multi-step business processes with limited supervision. This transition creates the agentic enterprise, in which AI systems function as operational business actors even though they remain incapable of bearing moral blame, legal duties, or institutional responsibility. The resulting accountability gap appears when organizations delegate real authority to AI but cannot identify who authorized an action, which data and rules shaped it, who was expected to intervene, or how an affected person can obtain correction. This conceptual article examines that gap through business ethics, contemporary AI governance, organizational responsibility, and faith-informed public reason. It distinguishes functional agency from moral and legal agency and argues that responsibility must remain with identifiable human principals and deploying institutions. The article proposes an Enterprise Agent Accountability Framework with seven connected controls: named human ownership, bounded delegation, agent identity and authorization, traceable action records, risk-proportionate human review, stakeholder notice and appeal, and remedy with continuous learning. It also introduces a five-level autonomy model for matching controls to business risk and applies the framework to hiring, pricing, customer service, procurement, finance, marketing, and supply-chain operations. The study contributes an interdisciplinary governance model that links technical controls with dignity, justice, transparency, responsibility, and public benefit. It concludes that enterprises may delegate tasks and limited authority to AI agents, but they may not delegate away accountability.

W7223096281.abstract: Model compression makes large language models deployable, but today's evaluation tells an incomplete story. Standard practice measures retained task performance and stops there. This misses a critical fact: compression perturbs the distributed knowledge embedded across billions of weights, and task scores alone cannot reveal which underlying abilities survive and which quietly collapse. To solve this question, we introduce ACE-Compression, an ability-centric evaluation framework. Instead of asking only "does the compressed model still answer correctly?", we ask "which of its core abilities remain intact?" Our framework probes four deployment-facing dimensions: procedural reasoning and constraint execution, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition and affective understanding, and persona fidelity and stylistic consistency. Across more than 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs-covering quantization and pruning-we find that compression redistributes ability profiles. Coarse, local, and surface-level signals often persist, while fine-grained, long-tail, and context-dependent abilities become fragile. Quantization consistently outperforms pruning in retention, but the practical meaning of that gap depends entirely on which ability an application requires. Based on our findings, deployers can choose compression methods by the ability profile their application needs, not just by a leaderboard average. And algorithm designers gain diagnostic signals to build compression methods that preserve what matters. We believe that ACE-Compression turns compression from a black-box accuracy drop into an interpretable intervention-one we can measure, understand, and ultimately improve.

W7223103704.abstract: Empathetic interaction involves two distinguishable capacities: representing another person's emotional state (cognitive empathy) and generating an appropriate response to that state (affective empathy). We apply this distinction to examine how emotion-related information is internally organized, selectively attended to, and carried through response generation in Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct across 10 emotion categories from the EmpatheticDialogues dataset. Layer-wise linear probing revealed a broad middle-layer region of peak emotion-category decodability, with the layer-11 L2 probe achieving 63.6% held-out accuracy against a 10% chance level and a 54.6% TF-IDF lexical baseline. During response generation, emotion-related user tokens received 1.89 times as much attention per token as other utterance tokens, concentrated across layers 10-15. Target-emotion alignment then decreased from a mean cosine similarity of 0.239 for input representations to 0.125 for generated responses, with positive drift in 77% of examples and the largest shifts for angry and furious. Emotion-category representation, attention allocation, and response-level alignment therefore emerge as distinguishable components of model processing that can be analyzed through a functional cognitive-affective empathy framework. These findings provide a foundation for monitoring emotion representations during generation and leveraging models' existing affective structure to support more naturally empathetic responses without relying on external prompting or explicit emotion conditioning.

W7223113263.abstract: Abstract Within the military realm the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems, including Autonomous Weapons Systems (AWS), are more and more employed in the operational field. An expansion where scientific progress is not always accompanied by a comprehensive adaptation of existing international law to cyberspace, as is the case with International Humanitarian Law (IHL). Therefore, there is a need to establish a useful framework of Meaningful Human Control (MHC) in those systems, especially with regards to Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS). One possible way forward could be the use of Artificial Moral Agents (AMA), to overcome some of the difficulties that the use of AWS in military operations may impose on the adequate application of IHL. Our investigation explores the design of a conceptual framework for the use of AMA for AWS.
